word:lxx:L712225.explanation: This adjective describes people who have been called together or summoned. It points to a gathered group brought together by an intentional call, rather than people who happen to be present. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Numbers 16:2, so its precise force there depends on the surrounding passage. Its basic sense highlights the act of calling people together and their resulting status as an assembled group.

word:lxx:L712250.explanation: This verb means “gird”: to fasten or secure clothing or something around the body. It describes an action of preparation, allowing a person to move or work without loose clothing getting in the way. In the Greek Old Testament corpus, it occurs twice, once in Leviticus 8:7 and once in 1 Maccabees 3:3. The precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse, but the ordinary meaning remains the act of girding or fastening around oneself.

word:lxx:L712333.explanation: This adjective describes something plaited or woven together, with separate strands or parts joined into one connected whole. word:lxx:L712391.explanation: This noun describes “living with; intercourse”—shared life or close association between people. It can refer broadly to dwelling or being together, while in some uses it points to intimate intercourse. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs four times, all in deuterocanonical writings: once in Wisdom and three times in 3 Maccabees. Its exact force in any particular sentence depends on the surrounding words and subject being discussed.

word:lxx:L712452.explanation: Synepischyō means to join in supporting.

word:lxx:L712500.explanation: This verb means to say the same thing with someone else—to agree with that person. It describes shared verbal affirmation rather than merely being silent or inwardly favorable. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, at 4 Maccabees 13:1; the single reference identifies its location but does not by itself establish the verse’s full contextual force. Its basic sense is joining another person’s expressed position.

word:lxx:L712575.explanation: Sphallō means to make fall or throw down.

word:lxx:L712618.explanation: Sōba, also rendered Sova, is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies a person or place by name rather than describing an action, quality, or object. This name occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament, appearing once each in 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, and Psalms. word:lxx:L712621.explanation: Sōbak, also rendered Sovak, is a proper name referring to a person. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in 2 Samuel: 10:16 and 10:18. word:lxx:L712683.explanation: Tabeēl, also given as Tavil, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a person in the Greek Old Testament tradition. Without the surrounding verse text, its personal identity cannot be explained further; the lexical evidence establishes the name itself, not the person’s character, role, or significance in those passages.

word:lxx:L712746.explanation: This Greek LXX adjective means “quickest,” describing someone or something that acts, moves, or happens with greater speed than others. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its basic meaning remains the superlative idea of being quickest.

word:lxx:L712863.explanation: Timōria means punishment or castigation. It can also refer to vengeance.

word:lxx:L712966.explanation: This adjective means “on the third day,” identifying something by its timing. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its basic meaning is a time reference: something occurring or existing on the third day.

word:lxx:L712984.explanation: Trophē means nourishment. It can also refer to provisions.

word:lxx:L713002.explanation: This verb means “have a hole.” It describes the condition of something that contains an opening or perforation. The surrounding words and verse determine what object has the opening, but the verb itself expresses that condition rather than naming the object or explaining why the hole exists.

word:lxx:L713154.explanation: Hyperoraō means to overlook. A command not to overlook a wandering animal requires turning it back to its owner.

word:lxx:L713288.explanation: Hypsos means height. It can also refer to what is high.

word:lxx:L713330.explanation: Phalet, also rendered Falet, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a person in the Greek Old Testament tradition. word:lxx:L713345.explanation: Phanouēl is a proper name. It is used for both a city and a man.

word:lxx:L713406.explanation: Pheidomai means to spare. It can also mean to refrain.

word:lxx:L713543.explanation: Phollathi, also rendered “Follathi,” is a proper name rather than a general word with an abstract meaning. It functions as a name in the Greek Old Testament tradition. This form occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at 1 Chronicles 26:5. Because no verse text or surrounding context is available here, its specific historical role cannot be explained beyond identifying the proper name itself.

word:lxx:L713648.explanation: Chabasin is a proper name, rendered also as Khavasin. It does not describe an action, quality, or general idea; it identifies a particular named person or place in the Greek Old Testament text. This name occurs once in the LXX corpus, at Jeremiah 42:3. Without the surrounding verse text, its specific identity cannot be clarified further, but its basic function is that of a name rather than an ordinary descriptive word.

word:lxx:L713671.explanation: Chalasta means a festoon or an ornamental chain.

word:lxx:L713785.explanation: This adjective describes something as “wintry” or “stormy,” expressing the character of unsettled weather. The word’s central idea is weather marked by winter or storm, while the surrounding verse determines exactly what it describes there.

word:lxx:L713824.explanation: Chenara, also rendered Khenara, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. Because it functions as a name, its meaning is primarily its identification of a particular place or named entity, not a general concept that can be translated into an ordinary English definition.

word:lxx:L713910.explanation: χορεύω means “dance a round”: it describes the action of moving in a circle or group dance. As a verb, it expresses dancing rather than naming a person, place, or object. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs four times: three times in Old Testament books and once in 4 Maccabees. Its basic sense remains focused on dancing in a rounded or joined movement, while the surrounding verse determines the particular occasion.

word:lxx:L713965.explanation: Chriō means to anoint, applying oil to a person or object.

word:lxx:L714173.explanation: Ōphir is a proper name, functioning as the name “Ōphir” or “Ofir.” It does not describe an action, quality, or ordinary object, but identifies what is named by this title.
